newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Christmas bomber tormented by son's suicide.
newsitem.headline: German Christmas bomber tormented by son's suicide.

text.p: German police said on Friday a Frankfurt woman who killed herself and two other women in a Christmas Eve grenade explosion in a church had been haunted by the suicide of her 18-year-old son seven years ago.

The 49-year-old woman, who detonated two hand grenades strapped to her abdomen during a packed midnight service, had been in psychiatric care ever since her son threw himself under a train near the church in 1989.
"She was not able to come to terms with the death of her son," said Frankfurt police spokesman Manfred Feist. "She wasn't able to cope with the loss and apparently wanted to follow him into death."
Police identified the two grenades that killed the three women and injured 13 other worshippers as M-52 models, believed made in Yugoslavia.
With a political motive ruled out, police were focusing their investigation on how the woman had obtained the grenades.
"These explosives are being offered on the black market," Feist said. "Anyone really determined could probably have obtained these grenades without any special connections."

The two other dead women, sisters aged 59 and 61, were sitting in front of the bomber in a rear pew when the blast shook the small stone Protestant church in the western Frankfurt district of Sindlingen shortly before midnight on Tuesday.
The 13 injured, who included a 12-year-old girl, were caught in a wave of shrapnel and splinters of pews shattered by the blast.
Most of those hurt were no longer in critical condition on Friday, but authorities said it was still uncertain whether the mother of the 12-year-old girl, a church worker, would survive.
Police did not release the name of the suicide bomber, but the tabloid daily Bild identified her as Heidrun-Erika J. The paper, following German tradition, did not publish her surname.
It said she had been separated from her husband and nine-year-old daughter.
Investigators said they believed the woman apparently did not intend to kill other people because witnesses said she was leaning forward in a crouched position when she triggered the grenades.
They said a search of her apartment in the outlying town of Usingen had also supported that conclusion.
"Based on all the evidence we have collected...it appears that she wanted to kill only herself," Feist said.
After her son's death, the woman moved with her husband and young daughter to another Frankfurt district. She then moved by herself to the outlying town of Usingen in October 1995.

Police would not comment on media reports that the woman may have got the idea for the bombing from a film recently shown on German television in which a man blew himself up in the middle of a Christmas church service.
